bread-wheat-or-cracked-wheat-toasted.title: Bread, wheat or cracked wheat, toasted

content.title: About
content.content: Toasted bread made from whole wheat or cracked wheat is a dry, crunchy product obtained by applying heat to whole grains. It has a distinctive nutty aroma and is used as a snack, a garnish, or an ingredient in various dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Toasting intensifies the wheat aroma and creates a crisp texture.
Traditionally this product has been used in Armenian and Georgian cuisines as a light snack.
Toasted wheat bread is often added to soups and stews for extra body.
It can serve as a gluten‑free breadcrumb alternative when made from gluten‑free wheat varieties.
In some regions it is known as “cracked wheat croutons.”

items.title: Rich in dietary fiber
items.content: The toasting process retains most of wheat’s fiber, which supports healthy digestion.

items.title: Source of complex carbohydrates
items.content: Complex carbs provide sustained energy, beneficial for active individuals.

items.title: Contains B‑vitamins
items.content: Wheat supplies thiamine, niacin, and vitamin B6, important for metabolism.

items.title: Mineral content
items.content: Provides magnesium, phosphorus, and iron, which are essential for bones and blood formation.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Toasting without added oil keeps the product virtually fat‑free.

items.title: Wheat allergy
items.content: People with wheat allergy or celiac disease should avoid this product.

items.title: High glycemic index
items.content: Thermal processing raises the glycemic index, so portion control is advised for diabetics.

items.title: Acrylamide formation
items.content: Toasting can generate small amounts of acrylamide, a potential carcinogen; moderate consumption is recommended.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Enjoy toasted wheat bread as a snack, sprinkle it over salads, soups, yogurt, or cottage cheese, or grind it into crunchy breadcrumbs for coating or topping.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in an airtight container in a cool, dry place away from moisture and direct sunlight. For longer shelf life, keep it in the refrigerator to maintain crispness and prevent rancidity.

chow-fun-noodles-with-vegetables-meatles.title: Chow fun noodles with vegetables, meatless

content.title: About
content.content: Chow fun noodles with vegetables, meatless is a rice‑flour noodle stir‑fry with a mix of vegetables and aromatic spices, containing no meat. The dish provides carbohydrates, vitamins and minerals from carrots, broccoli, bell peppers and other vegetables.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Chow fun is a traditional Southeast Asian dish popular in China, Vietnam and Thailand.
The noodles are made from rice flour, making them gluten‑free and suitable for people with celiac disease.
The vegetarian version often uses soy sauce and plant oils instead of meat while retaining a rich flavor.
Traditionally the noodles are wide and flat, which helps them hold sauce and vegetables better.
The dish cooks quickly: stir‑frying takes about 5‑7 minutes.

items.title: Source of complex carbs
items.content: Rice noodles provide sustained energy release, helping maintain stable blood sugar levels.

items.title: Rich in vitamins
items.content: The vegetable mix supplies vitamin C, vitamin K, folate and beta‑carotene, supporting immunity and skin health.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Absence of meat and moderate use of plant oils make the dish heart‑friendly.

items.title: Gluten‑free
items.content: Rice noodles are suitable for those with gluten intolerance.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Fiber from the vegetables aids bowel function and promotes satiety.

items.title: Soy sauce allergy
items.content: If soy sauce is used, individuals with soy allergy may experience reactions.

items.title: Sodium content
items.content: Prepared product may contain elevated salt levels; people with hypertension should monitor portion size.

items.title: Food safety risk
items.content: Improper storage of the cooked noodles above 4 °C for more than 2 hours can allow bacterial growth.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: The dish is ready after reheating in a pan or microwave. Add fresh herbs, lime juice or nuts for extra flavor.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store in the refrigerator at 0‑4 °C in an airtight container for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in bags at –18 °C.

content.title: About
content.content: Tilapia is a freshwater fish from the cichlid family, widely farmed in aquaculture. Steamed tilapia retains a delicate flavor, low fat content, and most of its nutrients.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Tilapia is one of the most affordable and fast‑growing fish worldwide.
Unlike many marine species, tilapia can thrive in freshwater and intensive farming systems.
Steaming preserves up to 90 % of vitamin B12, essential for the nervous system.
Its mild white flesh makes it popular in children’s meals.
In some regions the fish is called “African fish,” although its origin is Southeast Asian rivers.

items.title: Low in fat
items.content: Steamed tilapia contains less than 2 g of fat per 100 g, making it suitable for low‑fat diets.

items.title: Rich source of protein
items.content: A 100‑g serving provides about 20 g of high‑quality protein needed for tissue growth and repair.

items.title: Contains vitamin D
items.content: Vitamin D in tilapia aids calcium absorption and supports bone health.

items.title: Source of selenium
items.content: Selenium acts as an antioxidant and supports immune function.

items.title: Rich in B‑vitamins
items.content: Vitamins B6 and B12 help maintain energy metabolism and nervous system health.

items.title: Water quality control
items.content: Tilapia raised in polluted water can accumulate toxins; choose products from reputable farms.

items.title: Fish allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to fish, including tilapia.

items.title: Omega‑6 fatty acids
items.content: Tilapia contains more omega‑6 than omega‑3 fatty acids, so balance the diet with other omega‑3 sources.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Steamed tilapia can be served with lemon, herbs (parsley, dill) and a light yogurt sauce. It works well in salads, rice dishes, or as a filling for wraps.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep fresh tilapia refrigerated at 0‑2 °C, wrapped in plastic, for up to 2 days. Frozen fillets store at –18 °C for up to 3 months.

content.title: About
content.content: Chocolate ice cream is a frozen dessert made from milk, cream, sugar and cocoa mass or chocolate chips. It features a smooth, creamy flavor with a pronounced chocolate note and a characteristic velvety texture.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The first chocolate‑flavored ice cream appeared in the United States in the early 20th century.
Chocolate ice cream is often used as a base for ice‑cream suflés and milkshakes.
Dark chocolate in the recipe increases antioxidant content compared with plain vanilla ice cream.
In many countries, nuts or caramel pieces are added for extra texture.
There is a “soft‑serve” version that is served immediately after freezing, without a hardening period.

items.title: Source of antioxidants
items.content: Cocoa mass contains flavonoids that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Provides calcium
items.content: Dairy ingredients supply calcium, essential for bones and teeth.

items.title: Energy boost
items.content: Combines carbohydrates and fats for a quick source of energy.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: Milk and chocolate provide vitamin B12 and riboflavin, supporting the nervous system.

items.title: Mood improvement
items.content: Chocolate stimulates serotonin production, which can enhance mood.

items.title: High sugar content
items.content: Excessive consumption may contribute to weight gain and increase diabetes risk.

items.title: Lactose intolerance
items.content: Contains dairy, which can cause discomfort for those who are lactose intolerant.

items.title: Allergy to cocoa or milk
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions.

items.title: Caloric density
items.content: A typical serving (100 g) contains about 200–250 kcal.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve chocolate ice cream in cones, cups, or as part of desserts such as cakes, parfaits, and milkshakes. It pairs well with berries, nuts, caramel sauce, or a sprinkle of grated chocolate.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Keep ice cream in a freezer at –18 °C (0 °F) or lower. After opening, store in an airtight container to prevent absorption of other odors. Do not thaw and refreeze.

content.title: About
content.content: Onion (Allium cepa) is a biennial herb cultivated for its edible bulb. Raw onion has a sharp, slightly sweet flavor and a crunchy texture. It is used fresh in salads, sauces, marinades, and as an aromatic base in many dishes.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Onion belongs to the Amaryllidaceae family and is a close relative of garlic, leeks, and shallots.
There are over 600 onion varieties differing in color (yellow, red, white) and taste.
Raw onion contains sulfur compounds that release volatile gases when cut, causing tears.
In ancient Egypt, onions symbolized immortality and were used in rituals.
Properly stored onion bulbs can last for several months.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Onion provides quercetin and sulfur compounds that help protect cells from oxidative stress.

items.title: Supports cardiovascular health
items.content: Phytochemicals in onion may lower cholesterol levels and improve vessel function.

items.title: Contains vitamin C
items.content: Vitamin C boosts immunity and participates in collagen synthesis.

items.title: May help regulate blood sugar
items.content: Sulfur compounds and flavonoids can improve insulin sensitivity.

items.title: Source of fiber
items.content: Dietary fiber supports digestive health and promotes satiety.

items.title: Allergy
items.content: Some individuals may experience allergic reactions to onion, ranging from skin rashes to swelling.

items.title: Stomach irritation
items.content: Raw onion can increase stomach acidity and cause discomfort in people with gastritis or ulcers.

items.title: Gas and bloating
items.content: Sulfur compounds may lead to increased gas production and abdominal bloating.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Large amounts of onion can enhance the effect of anticoagulants, so moderation is advised for those on blood‑thinners.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Raw onion is added to salads, sandwiches, guacamole, marinades, and sauces. It can be finely diced, sliced, or grated. Soaking sliced onion in cold water for 10‑15 minutes reduces its sharpness.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store onions in a cool, dry, dark, well‑ventilated place. Proper conditions keep them fresh for 2‑3 months. Do not refrigerate onions with potatoes, as they accelerate each other's spoilage.

content.title: About
content.content: Sopaipilla is a fried dough pastry traditional to Latin American cuisine, especially in Chile, Argentina and Peru. Made from simple ingredients—flour, water, salt and leavening—it has a soft, slightly crisp exterior and an airy interior. This version is served without syrup or honey to highlight the natural dough flavor.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Sopaipillas are often filled with cheese, meat or vegetables.
In Chile they are called “sopaipilla,” while in Peru they are known as “churros” (not to be confused with the Spanish churro).
The dough is mixed quickly and fried immediately, giving a fresh, puffed texture.
Traditionally sold at street stalls as a warm, comforting snack in cooler weather.
They can be made sweet (with sugar) or savory; this description focuses on the unsweetened version.

items.title: Source of carbohydrates
items.content: Sopaipilla provides a quick source of energy thanks to the carbohydrates in the dough.

items.title: Low fat content
items.content: When fried in a modest amount of oil, it remains relatively low‑calorie compared with other fried pastries.

items.title: Contains fiber
items.content: Whole‑grain flour used in traditional recipes adds dietary fiber that supports digestion.

items.title: B‑vitamins
items.content: The dough supplies small amounts of B1, B2 and niacin, which aid metabolism.

items.title: Easy to digest
items.content: Its simple composition makes sopaipilla gentle on the stomach for most people.

items.title: Gluten allergy
items.content: Sopaipilla is made with wheat flour and is not suitable for people with celiac disease or gluten sensitivity.

items.title: Frying oil
items.content: Using excessive oil can make the pastry high in calories and introduce trans fats.

items.title: Serving temperature
items.content: Very hot sopaipilla can burn the mouth and esophagus, especially in children.

items.title: Salt content
items.content: If salt is added, monitor the amount to avoid excessive sodium intake.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Sopaipilla can be enjoyed plain as a snack, split open and stuffed with cheese, meat, beans or vegetables. It is also served with avocado sauce, salsa, or a yogurt dip.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store cooked sopaipilla in an airtight container at room temperature for up to 1‑2 days. For longer storage, refrigerate up to 5 days or freeze for up to 1 month. Reheat in the oven before serving to restore crispness.

content.title: About
content.content: Pepperpot Soup (1899) is a traditional thick spiced soup that first appeared at the turn of the 20th century. It is made with beef broth, ginger root, cinnamon, cloves, pepper, and sweet potatoes. The result is a richly aromatic, mildly hot broth characteristic of colonial‑influenced cuisine.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: First mentioned in culinary journals in 1899, which gave the dish its name.
Originally served in ceramic pots that retained heat and flavor.
The classic recipe used cassava root instead of sweet potatoes.
Often provided as a “morning fuel” for mining communities because it stays hot for hours.
Some regional variations add coconut milk to mellow the heat.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Spices such as cinnamon and cloves contain polyphenols that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports digestion
items.content: Ginger and pepper stimulate gastric secretions and aid digestive processes.

items.title: Source of vitamin C
items.content: Sweet potatoes and tomatoes provide vitamin C, which boosts immune function.

items.title: Contains iron
items.content: Beef broth and meat supply easily absorbable iron beneficial for blood health.

items.title: Moderately caloric
items.content: The soup is satiating yet, when eaten in reasonable portions, does not lead to over‑consumption.

items.title: Spicy heat
items.content: High amounts of pepper can irritate the stomach of people with gastritis.

items.title: Spice allergies
items.content: Some individuals may be sensitive to cinnamon, cloves, or ginger.

items.title: High sodium content
items.content: Commercial broth often contains a lot of salt; low‑sodium versions are recommended.

items.title: Calorie boost from coconut milk
items.content: Adding coconut milk raises the calorie count and saturated fat level.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Serve the soup hot, often with chunks of bread or flatbreads. Garnish with fresh herbs, a squeeze of lime, or a dollop of sour cream to soften the heat.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Cool the soup to room temperature, then store in an airtight container in the refrigerator for up to 3 days. For longer storage, freeze in portions for up to 2 months. Stir well before reheating.

content.title: About
content.content: Tea, iced, bottled, black, unsweetened is a ready‑to‑drink beverage made from black tea leaves that have been extracted, filtered and chilled. No added sugar means the natural bitterness and aroma of black tea remain, along with a low calorie count.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: Black tea is rich in polyphenols that may act as antioxidants.
Iced tea is a popular summer refreshment because it quenches thirst quickly.
Bottle packaging protects the drink from light and preserves flavor longer than glass.
Being sugar‑free makes it suitable for people monitoring blood glucose levels.
Cold black tea retains some caffeine, providing a mild energy boost.

items.title: Rich in antioxidants
items.content: Black tea contains catechins and theaflavins that help combat free radicals.

items.title: Supports heart health
items.content: Moderate regular consumption of black tea is linked to improved vascular function.

items.title: Low in calories
items.content: The absence of sugar makes the drink virtually calorie‑free, useful for weight management.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Iced tea contributes to fluid intake, especially in hot weather.

items.title: May improve mental alertness
items.content: Caffeine content can enhance concentration and alertness.

items.title: Caffeine sensitivity
items.content: People sensitive to caffeine may experience nervousness, insomnia, or rapid heartbeat.

items.title: Possible acidity
items.content: Black tea can increase stomach acidity, which may be problematic for gastritis sufferers.

items.title: Interaction with medications
items.content: Caffeine can amplify the effects of certain drugs, such as CNS stimulants.

items.title: Storage conditions
items.content: Prolonged exposure to heat can cause the drink to lose flavor and aroma.

items.title: Allergic reactions
items.content: Rarely, some individuals may be allergic to components of tea.

content.title: How to Eat
content.content: Iced black tea unsweetened is ready to drink straight from the bottle. It can be enjoyed on its own, used in cocktails, mixed with fruit juices, or served over ice with a slice of lemon.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store the bottle in a cool, dark place. Once opened, keep it refrigerated and consume within 3–5 days.

content.title: About
content.content: Tom Collins is a classic highball cocktail made with gin, fresh lemon juice, simple syrup and sparkling water. It is served over ice in a tall glass and typically garnished with a lemon slice or a cherry.

content.title: Interesting Facts
items: The drink originated in the United States in the mid‑19th century and is named after popular bartender John Thomas Collins.
The original recipe called for only gin, lemon juice and sugar; carbonated water was added later.
Tom Collins is considered a predecessor of the sweeter Gin Fizz and the Cuba Libre.
Variations exist with whiskey (Whiskey Collins) or rum (Rum Collins).
It is traditionally served in a highball glass of 300–350 ml capacity.

items.title: Vitamin C
items.content: Fresh lemon juice provides vitamin C, which supports the immune system and acts as an antioxidant.

items.title: Moderate alcohol content
items.content: When prepared with proper proportions, the cocktail contains a moderate amount of alcohol, which can promote relaxation without heavy intoxication.

items.title: Hydration
items.content: Sparkling water and ice help maintain fluid balance, especially on hot days.

items.title: Alcohol
items.content: Like any alcoholic beverage, Tom Collins can cause intoxication, interact with medications, and is contraindicated during pregnancy.

items.title: Sugar content
items.content: Simple syrup adds a notable amount of sugar, which may be undesirable for people with diabetes or low‑glycemic diets.

items.title: Acidity
items.content: Lemon juice increases acidity and may irritate the stomach in individuals with gastritis or reflux.

content.title: How to Make
content.content: In a shaker combine 50 ml gin, 25 ml freshly squeezed lemon juice and 15 ml simple syrup. Add ice, shake vigorously, then strain into a tall glass filled with ice and top with sparkling water. Garnish with a lemon slice or a cherry.

content.title: Storage
content.content: Store ingredients separately: gin in a cool dark place, lemons in the refrigerator, simple syrup in a sealed bottle in the fridge for up to a week. Use sparkling water shortly after opening.
